prompt: With IAM Identity Center in place, where does a person's login live?
hint: Not in any of the accounts.

choices.text: In an IAM user created in each account the person works in
choices.why: That is the arrangement Identity Center replaces: one user per person per account, each to create and delete.

choices.text: In the one identity source, outside every account
choices.why: Right. The accounts hold roles; the person is in the Identity Center directory, Active Directory or an external provider.

choices.text: In the management account, as an IAM user with a role in each account
choices.why: Identity Center creates no IAM users at all, in the management account or anywhere else.

choices.text: In `~/.aws/credentials`, on the laptop the person works from
choices.why: That file holds keys. A sign-in through Identity Center leaves only a cached token, and only for the session.

prompt: The shop connects Google Workspace to Identity Center. What is SCIM's job in that connection, as opposed to SAML's?
hint: One protocol is about the moment of signing in; the other is not.

choices.text: Checking the person's password and second factor at sign-in
choices.why: Google checks those, and SAML carries the result to Identity Center as a signed assertion.

choices.text: Encrypting the assertion so that no password reaches AWS
choices.why: No password reaches AWS in either protocol. The assertion is signed, and that is SAML's part.

choices.text: Keeping the users and groups current, before and after sign-ins
choices.why: Right. SAML says who is signing in now; SCIM says who exists and in which groups, before and after.

choices.text: Handing the command line its role credentials after each sign-in
choices.why: The command line gets role credentials from the portal with its cached token. SCIM runs between Google and Identity Center.

prompt: Somebody adds a policy by hand to the role `AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_…` inside `shop-prod`. What becomes of the change?
hint: Who manages that role?

choices.text: It spreads to every other account that has the same permission set
choices.why: Changes flow from the permission set to the roles, never from one role back to the others.

choices.text: It is overwritten the next time the permission set is provisioned to that account
choices.why: Right. Until then this one account quietly disagrees with the others, which is the worse half of it.

choices.text: IAM refuses it: the role can only be read inside the account
choices.why: Edits are possible, which is exactly why the rule against them has to be stated.

choices.text: It becomes part of the permission set itself
choices.why: The permission set is defined in Identity Center, not read back from the roles it provisioned.

prompt: The shop has six accounts and five people. With one IAM user per person in every account, how many IAM users would there be to audit?
hint: People times accounts.

prompt: Match each identity source to the organisation it fits.
hint: Three rows of the section's table.

pairs.right: a small team with no directory of its own
people who already sign in at Google or Entra ID

right_distractors: a program that runs outside AWS

prompt: Google is connected by SAML only, with no SCIM. `caio` leaves and is disabled in Google. What is left on the AWS side?
hint: Separate signing in from existing.

choices.text: Nothing: disabling him in Google deletes him everywhere
choices.why: Deleting him in Identity Center is SCIM's job, and there is no SCIM here.

choices.text: A user who can still sign in, since Identity Center keeps its own password for him
choices.why: With an external provider, Identity Center holds no password. Every sign-in goes to Google, which now refuses him.

choices.text: His user, groups and assignments, which cannot be used and still need deleting
choices.why: Right. SAML stops the sign-in; only SCIM, or somebody remembering, removes what is left.

choices.text: An IAM user in each account he was assigned to
choices.why: Assignments provision roles, not users. There were never IAM users for him.

prompt: What three things make up an account assignment?
hint: The triple of the section.

choices.text: A user or group, a permission set, and one account
choices.why: Right. Each assignment is one cell of the grid, and one role in that account.

choices.text: A role, a trust policy, and a permission policy
choices.why: Those are what a provisioned role is made of. The assignment is what causes it.

choices.text: A user, a password, and a second factor
choices.why: Those belong to the identity source. An assignment says nothing about how a person signs in.

choices.text: A permission set, an organisational unit, and a region
choices.why: An assignment targets one account, and a permission set is valid in every region of it.

prompt: Why does the section assign permission sets to the group `developers` rather than to `bia` directly?
hint: Count the commands for the next developer.

choices.text: Because Identity Center refuses assignments to users
choices.why: `--principal-type USER` is accepted. The choice is about upkeep, not a refusal.

choices.text: Because groups get longer sessions than users do, whatever the set says
choices.why: The session length belongs to the permission set, whoever it is assigned to.

choices.text: So one membership replaces three assignments
choices.why: Right. Joining the group gives every cell of its row, and leaving it removes them together.

choices.text: Because SCIM can provision groups and not single users
choices.why: SCIM provisions users and groups alike. This lab has no SCIM at all.

prompt: A permission set whose sessions last four hours is created with `--session-duration ___`.
hint: An ISO 8601 duration.

prompt: `create-account-assignment` answered `SUCCEEDED`, yet `shop-prod` lists only `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`. What does the measurement show?
hint: Which side of Identity Center does moto imitate?

choices.text: That the role is created only when somebody first signs in
choices.why: In AWS the role exists once provisioning finishes, before anybody signs in. moto never creates it.

choices.text: That the assignment was made to the wrong account
choices.why: `list-account-assignments` for `shop-prod` names both groups, so the account is right.

choices.text: That moto records the assignments and never provisions the role AWS would create there
choices.why: Right. AWS would hold `AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_…` there; the lab covers the administrative side only.

choices.text: That `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` is the role Identity Center provisions
choices.why: That role was made with the account, by Organizations, before any assignment existed.

prompt: What is the longest session, in hours, that AWS accepts for a permission set?
hint: The section gives the range.

prompt: `caio` opens `shop-prod` with `ReadOnly`: `ReadOnlyAccess` plus the inline deny of `s3:GetObject` on `shop-backups/*`. Can he download a backup?
hint: Lesson 8's first rule of evaluation.

choices.text: Yes: `ReadOnlyAccess` allows `s3:GetObject` everywhere
choices.why: It does allow it, and an explicit deny beats any allow. The allow is not the end of the evaluation.

choices.text: No: the explicit deny wins over the managed policy's allow
choices.why: Right. He can still list the bucket, since only `GetObject` is refused.

choices.text: Only from the console, where inline policies are not applied
choices.why: The console signs the same requests with the same role. The deny applies to every client.

choices.text: It depends on which policy was attached first
choices.why: Evaluation has no order of attachment. An explicit deny wins wherever it sits.

prompt: Which of these did moto 5.2.3 answer as AWS would, in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: The administrative calls, and not what follows from them.

choices.text: Listing the Identity Center instance and its identity store
choices.why: Right. It even had one before anything was created.

choices.text: Creating a permission set with a managed and an inline policy
choices.why: Right. `describe-permission-set` returned the name and the session duration.

choices.text: Creating users, groups and memberships in the identity store
choices.why: Right. `list-users` and `list-groups` returned them with their ids.

choices.text: Creating the `AWSReservedSSO_` role in the assigned account
choices.why: That is the step moto leaves out: the account held only `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`.

choices.text: Signing in with `aws sso login`
choices.why: moto has no sign-in service: the first request, `RegisterClient`, answered 500.

prompt: In `~/.aws/config`, what does the `[sso-session shop]` section hold that the `[profile prod-readonly]` section does not?
hint: One section is the sign-in, the other a destination.

choices.text: The account id and the name of the permission set to open there
choices.why: Those are the destination, and they are in the profile.

choices.text: The portal's address, its region and the scope
choices.why: Right. One session serves every profile that names it, so one sign-in opens all of them.

choices.text: A copy of the cached token, refreshed at each sign-in
choices.why: The token lives in `~/.aws/sso/cache/`, never in the config file.

choices.text: The access key the session signs with
choices.why: There is no access key anywhere in this arrangement. That is its point.

prompt: `env.sh` exports test keys, yet `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile prod-readonly` stops with `Error loading SSO Token` instead of using them. Why?
hint: How was the profile named?

choices.text: Because the test keys expired when moto restarted
choices.why: `test` and `test` never expire; they are placeholders moto accepts until its checking is on.

choices.text: Because an `sso-session` profile disables every other provider for good, in every terminal
choices.why: Nothing is disabled for good. Without `--profile` the same terminal still uses the test keys.

choices.text: `--profile` takes the environment's keys out of the chain
choices.why: Right. The command line then has only the profile's way in, and that way needs a sign-in first.

choices.text: Because moto refused the keys for that account
choices.why: No request reached moto. The command line stopped before sending anything.

prompt: Put the steps of `aws sso login` against AWS in order, as AWS's documentation describes them.
hint: The registration comes before anybody types anything.
items: it prints an address and a code
the person signs in at the identity provider, with MFA
each command trades the token for role credentials
trap: The token can only be cached after the person has signed in and allowed the access.

prompt: `ReadOnly` has `PT4H`, and the Identity Center session lasts eight hours. Five hours after `aws sso login`, `caio` runs a command with `prod-readonly`. What happens?
hint: Two clocks, and only one of them has run out.

choices.text: The command line asks him to run `aws sso login` again
choices.why: That happens when the Identity Center session ends, at eight hours. Three are left.

choices.text: The command fails, since four hours is the most any credential may last
choices.why: Four hours limits each set of role credentials, not the sign-in. New ones can be fetched.

choices.text: It quietly trades the cached token for a new set of role credentials, without asking him
choices.why: Right. The first set expired at four hours; the token is still valid, so the `sso` provider fetches another.

choices.text: It falls back to the test keys that `env.sh` exports
choices.why: With `--profile` the environment's keys are out of the chain, and here they are not needed anyway.

prompt: `aws sso login` writes its token into `~/.aws/sso/___/`, and `aws sso logout` removes it.
hint: The directory the command line looked in before anybody signed in.

prompt: Match each setting of the lesson's `~/.aws/config` to what it names.
hint: Two belong to the session, two to the profile.
right_distractors: the IAM user to sign in as

prompt: The shop hires `edu`, a contractor, for three months to read logs in `shop-staging`. Which arrangement follows this lesson?
hint: Leaving should be one action.

choices.text: An IAM user in `shop-staging` with an access key, deleted at the end of the contract
choices.why: That works until somebody forgets the date, and the key works from anywhere until then. People are not on the list for IAM users.

choices.text: His own user in a group given `ReadOnly` in `shop-staging`, disabled at the end
choices.why: Right. He signs in with a second factor, his sessions expire, and disabling him ends every future sign-in.

choices.text: The credentials of `bia`'s `ReadOnly` session, shared with him for the three months
choices.why: Those expire within hours, and CloudTrail would name `bia` for everything he did.

choices.text: A new permission set made just for him, assigned in every account
choices.why: He needs one account, and `ReadOnly` already says what reading means. Every account is far wider than asked.

prompt: CloudTrail in `shop-staging` shows a bucket deleted by `arn:aws:sts::132607488945:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_Developer_…/bia`. What does the ARN tell you?
hint: Read it from the end.

choices.text: An IAM user called `bia` in `shop-staging` deleted it with her key
choices.why: An IAM user's ARN has `:user/` in it. `assumed-role` means a role session.

choices.text: The role `Developer` was edited by `bia` beforehand to allow the deletion
choices.why: Nothing in the ARN speaks of an edit. `PowerUserAccess` already allows deleting buckets.

choices.text: `bia`, signed in through Identity Center, used `Developer`
choices.why: Right. The role is the provisioned `Developer`, reached through the group's assignment, and the session carries her name.

choices.text: Somebody used the management account's credentials while signed in as `bia`
choices.why: The account in the ARN is `shop-staging`'s, and the role belongs to it.

prompt: A developer copies the short-lived credentials from the access portal into `~/.aws/credentials` every morning. What does the lesson offer instead?
hint: The same job, without the file.

choices.text: An IAM user, so the credentials last longer
choices.why: Lasting longer is the problem with a key, not a cure for copying.

choices.text: A longer session duration on the permission set
choices.why: That makes the copied secret valid for longer and leaves the copying in place.

choices.text: An `sso-session` profile and `aws sso login`
choices.why: Right. One sign-in fills the cache, and every command fetches fresh role credentials on its own.

choices.text: `credential_process` pointing at the portal's page
choices.why: `credential_process` runs a program, and a web page is not one. The `sso` provider already does this properly.
